history_event: A long war with a rival kingdom ended in a negotiated peace, but the border forts it left behind still mark the land and the old grudges still shape marriage and trade.
Horsemen from the eastern plains broke the realm's army in a single afternoon, and the tribute they imposed financed a generation of resentful rebuilding.
A fever that began in the river ports killed a third of the people in two summers, and whole villages were abandoned to the orchards that have since gone wild.
A trusted march lord opened a gate to a besieging army for a promise of marriage, and the realm has never trusted its border lords with the keys to anything since.
When the salt trade shifted to a rival port, a fifth of the realm's townsfolk walked away in one autumn, leaving streets that farmers now plow for turnips.
A child was said to have stopped a flood by holding up a hand at the riverbank, and the shrine built on that spot has drawn pilgrims and counterfeit relics ever since.
Three years of rain that never came emptied the granaries, and the crown's decision to feed the cities before the countryside is still quoted as an insult in market squares.
A dispute over whether the dead might be prayed for in the old tongue split the temple in two, and rival shrines on either side of the river still refuse to share festivals.
A fire that started in a candlemaker's cellar took the royal archive with it, and every land grant older than two generations is now argued from memory and forged copies.
Shepherds found a sealed stair beneath a collapsed hill and sold the location to a scholar, whose dig uncovered a cache of brass tablets no living tongue can read.
Two royal brothers divided the realm by treaty and then spent thirty years undoing the division, leaving a border drawn through orchards and a peasantry that pays taxes twice.
A sorcerer-king drained the marshes to grow a private garden, and the drained soil later became the only good farmland in the region, which the crown seized on a legal pretext.
A tax on looms sparked a weavers' revolt that held the capital for eleven days, and the guild charter won in the settlement still limits what the crown may levy.
An earthquake cracked the aqueduct that fed the hill city, and the quarter built over the leak has been sinking a hand's width every decade ever since.
A wandering preacher gathered an army of pilgrims to retake a ruined shrine, and though the campaign failed, the roads and bridges his followers built still carry grain to market.
Refugees fleeing a burning kingdom to the north were settled on empty border land, and their descendants still speak a dialect that marks them as outsiders in their own villages.
Silver was struck in the western hills and for a decade every criminal and gambler in the region came to spend it, leaving a city of wide streets and deep debts.
The high temple's oracle fell silent for a year and then spoke nonsense, and half the priesthood walked out, taking the temple's silver and its best singers with them.
A shepherd's vision on a hillside began a movement that outlived the temple that condemned it, and its meeting houses now stand where the old shrines were pulled down.
The palace guard chose the next three rulers and deposed two of them, and the great families have since kept their sons out of the guard out of fear of the precedent.
A fishing village at the river mouth grew into the realm's second city in four generations, and its old families still call the great families of the capital newcomers.
A queen spent her dowry on a road through the mountains, and the trade it drew made her husband's rivals rich enough to rebel against him twice.
The river provinces seceded over a levy and were reconquered in one season, but the reconquest cost more than the levy and is still taught as a warning against clever victories.
An heir was poisoned at his own betrothal feast, and the inquiry that followed ruined three noble houses, whose surviving children were raised in exile and returned with claims.
A working meant to end a drought instead called down a season of unseasonable frost, and the orchards that died have been replaced by pasture the heirs still dispute.
A circle of healers ended a plague by burning the houses of the infected and quarantining the wells, and the quarantine laws they wrote are still read aloud each spring.
A chancellor sold the realm's border passwords to three neighbors at once, and the purge that followed executed so many clerks that the tax rolls went uncollected for two years.
A people displaced by a distant war arrived with their herds and their smiths, and their ironwork was so good that the realm's own smiths petitioned to have them expelled, unsuccessfully.
A slow subsidence drowned a temple district's best fields over forty years, and the lake it made is now a smuggler's road between two unfriendly courts.
The court spent a decade staging plays about its own virtue while the provinces went unpaid, and the satire written by a dismissed clerk is still performed at fairs.
A diplomatic marriage was annulled after the bride's household was found to have forged its genealogy, and the scandal made the realm distrustful of foreign matches for a century.
Three kings spent the realm's treasure on a palace no one could afford to heat, and its unfinished east wing has served as a barracks, a granary, and a debtors' prison.
A cult bred a strain of wheat that ripened in winter and then burned every field of it, and the fear of winter grain has never quite left the farming villages.
The last keeper of a library died without an heir, and her apprentices sold the books by weight to a candle-maker, so the realm knows its own history only through what was quoted elsewhere.
Repeated raids by a hill clan were answered with a punitive expedition that marched too far, and the two-year war that followed ended with the clan holding better land than before.
A guild bought grain from overseas during a failed harvest and sold it at cost, and the favor it earned has kept its members on the city council ever since.
A cattle sickness emptied the pastures in two summers, and the herders who turned to raising pigs instead still regard cattle as a luxury and pigs as a livelihood.
Three claimants fought a nine-year war over a throne, and the settlement that ended it divided the offices of state so evenly that no ruler since has been able to act quickly.
A miner's shaft broke into a flooded cavern full of old bones, and the work stopped for a generation while priests argued over whether the dead had been drowned or buried.
A generation of banditry on the high road was ended by a bounty that made informers of the bandits' own families, and the villages along that road still keep their doors barred after dark.
A spring appeared at a shrine during a siege and the defenders held out three months longer, and though the water is ordinary now, the shrine still sells it in sealed jars.
A ruler moved whole villages to the frontier to farm land no one wanted, and the families who survived the first winters still call themselves the king's orphans.
A regime banned the study of old law and burned the commentaries, and the judges who memorized them in defiance became a secret tradition that still meets in cellars.
Quarantine broke down in the port when merchants bribed the gate wardens, and the resulting outbreak is blamed for the city's long hostility to foreign ships.
A neighbor conquered the realm in a single campaign and ruled it for two generations, and the taxes left by that occupation are still the basis of every land dispute in the province.
A fleet sent to break a blockade was lost in a storm within sight of the harbor, and the realm never again built ships large enough to challenge its neighbors at sea.
A canal dug by conscripted labor opened the dry interior to settlement, and the conscripts' descendants still hold the water rights that the crown granted their grandparents in lieu of pay.
A heresy that denied the sanctity of inherited office spread among the lesser clergy, and though it was suppressed, its slogans are still shouted at coronations by the poor.
A marriage alliance with a distant power brought a century of peace and a slow influx of foreign habits, and old families still measure status by which side of that match they descend from.
A victorious general returned from the frontier with his army and took the throne without a battle, and the precedent has made every later ruler nervous about leaving the capital.
A summer fire took four wards of the capital and the tax records with them, and the rebuilding was funded by a levy on the very merchants who had lost their shops.
A creature came down from the high valleys for three winters running, and the bounty hunters who finally killed it were paid in land that is now a village with its own militia.
A ruler's long madness was kept secret by his household while clerks forged his seal, and the laws passed in those years were repealed so unevenly that the realm still argues about them.
A peasant rising over a new mill tax burned three manor houses before it was put down, and the mill tax was quietly withdrawn, teaching every village what a torch is worth.
For thirty years the realm's judges sold their verdicts, and when the practice was exposed the public lost faith in courts so thoroughly that duels of honor returned.
A period of peace and cheap bread let a generation of painters and masons work without patrons looking over their shoulders, and the style they invented is imitated badly in every temple since.
A ruler thinned the coinage to pay a war and the prices that followed took a decade to settle, and the old full-weight coins are still hoarded and still trusted over anything struck since.
A popular temple singer was executed for sedition in a dispute over a hymn, and the crowd that rioted afterward has been commemorated by a festival the authorities would rather forget.
A mountain that had been quiet for centuries threw ash over the northern farms, and the refugees it displaced founded the market towns that now dominate that region's grain trade.
An alliance was dissolved when its terms were published by a clerk who had been paid to embarrass both parties, and the two realms have distrusted written treaties ever since.
A plague hospital built outside the walls was burned by frightened neighbors, and the site is still avoided at night, though children dare each other to touch its stones.
A king's favored son was passed over and raised a rebellion in the provinces, and the amnesty that ended it left the son's officers in charge of the very garrisons they had besieged.
A city under siege bought the aid of a sorcerer with a promise it could not keep, and the price he collected emptied the treasury and killed the men who had signed the agreement.
A surveyor's error put a valuable forest on the wrong side of a border, and the courts that tried the resulting case produced a body of law every later boundary dispute cites.
A blight of locusts stripped three harvests and drove the price of bread so high that the crown opened the royal granaries, emptying reserves it later needed for war.
Hunters following a wounded animal found a paved road through the hills that no map showed, and the trade route reopened along it repaid the realm's war debts within a generation.
A defeated army was rebuilt around common soldiers rather than noble officers, and the reforms that humiliated the great houses made the realm briefly unbeatable and permanently divided.
A temple claimed the right to tithe the whole realm and the crown answered by seizing its lands, and the settlement left every parish with two competing claims to its granary.
An exiled house returned after forty years with foreign backing and reclaimed its lands, and the tenants who had been resettled on those lands were simply told to pay a different lord.
A storm tide drowned the lowland farms in a single night, and the seawall built afterward by forced labor has held twice and failed once since.
Mercenaries unpaid for a season sacked the town they had been hired to defend, and no city since has hired a company without keeping its pay chest under guard.
A palace fire killed the royal family and left a distant cousin on the throne, and the regency that ruled in his name redistributed so many titles that nearly every noble house owes it something.
A wandering sorcerer taught the realm's midwives to read and left a book of remedies, and the book has been recopied so often that no two copies agree.
A sorcerer who had served three rulers was burned on a charge of treason, and the lesser mages who fled the realm took knowledge of the old workings with them.
A great hunt was called to clear the wolves that had taken children from the border farms, and the huntsmen who stayed on afterward became the core of the realm's forest guard.
A neighboring power closed its passes for six years, and local merchants learned to make what they had always bought, souring a friendship that had lasted generations.
A prophecy that the realm would fall when its bells cracked led the crown to cast every bell anew, and the foundry districts that grew around the work became the realm's richest quarter.
A curse was laid on the realm's coin by a cheated moneychanger, and although no one can prove it did anything, coins from that mint are still avoided.
A siege that lasted three years ended when a smuggler showed the attackers an unguarded drain, and the quarter built over that drain is still called the traitor's gate.
A ruler ordered every household counted and every field measured, and the tax rolls made that year are so accurate that later laws could be imposed without ever meeting the people they burdened.
history_peak: Granaries that could feed the whole region through two failed harvests.
Roads kept so well that a cart could cross the realm in nine days.
A war fleet that kept every river mouth in friendly hands.
Scholars who charted the stars and the tides with equal care.
Singers sent for from courts a month's ride beyond the border.
Laws written plainly enough that farmers could cite them by chapter.
Horse herds that made every neighboring cavalry look shabby.
Shrines that drew pilgrims from lands the realm had never conquered.
Masonry that has not shifted a finger's width in four centuries.
Markets that set the price of grain for a dozen lesser cities.
Border forts placed so that no raider ever reached open farmland.
Levy rolls that could put a thousand spears on the road in a week.
Canals that carried water uphill to terraces no one thought farmable.
Physicians who could set bones and cut for stone and keep the patient.
Coin trusted from the salt coast to the high passes.
Noble houses that competed in patronage instead of private war.
Libraries holding copies of works burned everywhere else in the region.
A crown whose word ended disputes between cities without an army.
Craftsmen whose glass and dyed cloth were sold in six ports.
history_failure: The great houses held back their levies, each waiting to see who would win.
No plan could be agreed on, so the realm committed to none of them.
Its priests called the crisis a judgment and forbade any resistance.
Its treasury was already pledged to a war that no longer mattered.
Its generals spent the campaign winning arguments instead of battles.
Its border lords had grown used to settling raids on their own terms.
Its people had not been paid, fed, or told the truth in years.
Its best soldiers were overseas, garrisoning a conquest nobody wanted.
Its laws required a council for every decision, and the council could not be convened.
Its craftsmen had been conscripted into a project that consumed them.
Its allies had been insulted once too often and simply stayed home.
Its grain reserves had been sold the year before to balance a ledger.
Its mages quarreled over precedence while the wards failed one by one.
Its heirs distrusted one another more than they feared the enemy.
Capital and provinces blamed each other for the previous defeat.
Loyal relatives replaced experienced officers, and the army paid for it.
Its faith had promised deliverance, and deliverance never came.
Its watch had been allowed to rot because nobody expected trouble.
Its people did not believe the danger until the gates were already burning.
history_survivors: They took to the high pastures and have stayed there ever since.
They were granted land on a frontier in exchange for military service.
They settled in a foreign city and grew rich in a trade their hosts despised.
They scattered into the hill villages and lost their own tongue in two generations.
They were sold into service and their grandchildren bought their freedom.
They kept a quarter of their old city and still live by its older customs.
They fled into the marsh country and became guides no outsider can follow.
They took service with the conquerors and were hated for it by everyone left.
They married into the new ruling house and quietly outlasted it.
They withdrew to a monastery and preserved their records in its scriptorium.
They wandered as tinkers and smiths until settled law drove them onto the roads.
They were scattered among ten villages and forbade their children to marry out.
They crossed the desert and were never heard from again by anyone who wrote.
They became a mercenary company and fought for the powers that had ruined them.
They fled to an island and kept their own laws there for three centuries.
They were resettled as a buffer against raiders and grew hard and suspicious.
They retreated into the old mines and reemerged as a separate people.
They joined a new religious movement and became its first adherents.
They refused to leave and were slowly reduced to a few stubborn households.
history_origin: A river changed course and moved a whole district's wealth to a neighbor.
A shipment of grain arrived spoiled and the merchants blamed each other.
A marriage contract was broken after the bride's family lost its fortune.
A temple relic was stolen and every shrine in the region was searched.
A levy was raised to pay for a war that never happened.
A border marker was moved during a single night of heavy rain.
A poor harvest coincided with a tax increase and a rumor of hoarding.
A healer was accused of poisoning a noble child and fled before trial.
A succession was disputed by two cousins with equally good claims.
A road was closed for repairs and left a trade town without customers.
A sorcerer's experiment fouled a well that three villages drew from.
A mercenary company was dismissed without pay at the end of a campaign.
A ship carrying refugees was turned away from a harbor that needed labor.
A grant of land was confirmed twice, to two different families.
original_inhabitants: They were gone before the first settlers arrived, leaving only field boundaries.
They were killed or driven off in a war that took two generations to finish.
They were absorbed so completely that only a few words of their speech remain.
They were pushed into the least fertile hills and still farm there.
They became the new rulers by marrying into the incoming houses.
They were reduced to tenants on land their families had cleared.
They kept their own courts in three valleys and answer to no one else.
They mixed with the newcomers but kept their burial customs.
They fled across the water and their descendants still raid the coast.
They survived as a servant caste that no one will name aloud.
They were hired as soldiers and settled as a separate quarter in every town.
They were converted, renamed, and taught to forget their own genealogies.
They were wiped out by sickness before any treaty could be made.
No two accounts agree whether they fled, died, or were simply absorbed.
They held the highland passes and charged tolls until the passes were abandoned.
They were resettled by decree and their old villages were given to soldiers.
crisis_overcome: A single leader held the factions together long enough to outlast the danger.
The cities agreed to share grain and troops under a temporary council.
They endured, eating seed corn and burying their dead without ceremony.
Their faith gave them a reason to keep the walls manned through the winter.
A working of ward and wardstone turned the enemy's own weather against it.
A small, well-drilled force broke the siege before the main army arrived.
A marriage and a border adjustment bought them a decade of peace.
They dug canals, rebuilt bridges, and paid for it with three years of hunger.
They borrowed heavily, traded their way out, and repaid every creditor.
They gave up a province and a generation of pride to save the rest.
They made a bargain with a local power that everyone agreed never to discuss.
They abandoned the outer districts and held the river line instead.
A merchant league lent them the money at terms that crippled them for years.
They let the plague burn through the outer wards and sealed the inner ones.
They won by refusing battle and letting the invaders starve in the field.
They sacrificed their own fleet to block the harbor and saved the city.
dungeon_reaction: As hostile as the situation allows, and they move to attack or drive the party off at once.
Wary and unfriendly, weapons ready, with no patience for questions or delays.
Cautious and neutral, willing to talk while keeping one eye on the road behind them.
Well disposed and willing, glad to trade news, goods, or directions without much pressing.
Genuinely friendly and helpful, and they share what little they have as far as their means allow.
monster_shape: A tall, gaunt humanoid with too many joints.
A low, broad beast that moves on six legs.
A serpent body ending in a cluster of small arms.
A writhing mass of pale, rootlike tendrils.
A winged thing with a broken, hunched back.
A segmented crawler the length of a cart.
A bloated, floating sac trailing fine threads.
A human frame wrapped in layered hide plates.
A many-eyed head on a spidery walking body.
A horned quadruped with a flattened, toadlike face.
A swarm of finger-sized things acting as one.
A tall, thin giant with limbs too long for its body.
A translucent, fishlike shape that hovers above ground.
A squat, armored form with no visible head.
A quadruped with a human face and no eyes.
A pillar of woven reeds and bone that walks.
A soft, shapeless thing that borrows the shape of what it eats.
A pale, hairless biped that walks on its knuckles.
A branching, antlered shape with a hollow chest cavity.
monster_drive: To keep every intruder out of its ground.
To seed new broods in living hosts.
To gather and guard bright metal.
A deep hatred of anyone who carries fire.
To obey the last order it was given.
To see what happens when things break.
To complete a rite it was made for.
To drink from a particular spring.
To avenge a death it cannot name.
An urge no living thing can explain.
To be worshipped by something weaker.
To return to a place that no longer exists.
To collect the voices of the dying.
To keep its young fed and hidden.
To follow the scent of old blood.
To prevent something from being opened.
To find a mate that no longer exists.
monster_twist: It mimics the voice of whoever last spoke to it.
It refuses to cross running water but will wait for days.
It heals quickly from any wound it did not see coming.
It is two creatures sharing one skin, and they disagree.
It collects small objects and trades them for food.
It will not attack anyone who is singing.
It casts no shadow and grows agitated in bright sun.
It follows orders given by anyone wearing a crown.
It remembers every face it has seen and greets them by name.
Its blood hardens into a brittle, glassy shell.
It can only move toward what it can smell.
It repeats the last action it saw performed, exactly.
It is blind but hunts by the sound of breathing.
It sleeps in the shape of a stone and wakes when struck.
It cannot tell the living from the dead.
It is bound to a single room and cannot leave it.
It sheds its skin when frightened, and the skin keeps moving.
It offers a bargain before it attacks.
It is terrified of its own reflection.
It speaks only in questions and answers them itself.
It grows larger each time it is wounded.
It has learned to open doors and does so politely.
It prefers the company of animals to people.
It leaves a trail of frost that melts by noon.
It will stop fighting to rescue a fallen companion.
It counts everything it sees and becomes furious at errors.
It can step through shadows but not into light.
It imitates the wounded cries of animals to draw people out.
It has a second mouth that speaks a language of its own.
It will not enter a place it has not been invited.
It is dying of something and knows it.
It gives away its treasure to anyone who asks politely.
